reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an Ethereum MEV bot as an easy passive-income opportunity, claiming returns of up to 10 ETH or $20,000 per day when viewers deploy it. Viewers are instructed to deposit at least 0.25 ETH into the contract or bot address, with larger deposits presented as producing more profit. Although the presentation includes educational and high-risk disclaimers and the pending 1 ETH interaction has no established outcome, the promotion remains directly tied to the required cryptocurrency funding.

citations.quote: Today I'll be teaching you step-by-step how to deploy an Ethereum Trading Bot I've recently developed in the Solidity language which can make you very easy daily passive income
Deposit funds (at least 0.25 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
the more you put in the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich, and the more profit you'll be able to accumulate over time
This will enable the bot to start snipe the mempool to find different liquidity pairs in order for you to sandwich transactions.
It takes advantage of decentralized finance platforms, such asiswap to sandwich transactions for arbitrage.

opening.argument: Judge the income claims alongside the video's explicit limits. The description calls the material educational, warns that cryptocurrency carries a considerable risk of loss, and says no particular outcome is guaranteed. The suggested funding amount is explained in terms of gas and burn fees, not presented as a threshold that assures profit. Even if the speaker's reported results are striking, the surrounding warnings leave room for a risky trading demonstration rather than a promise that viewers will earn the same return.

citations.quote: All content is purely for educational purposes and reflect the speaker(s) personal opinions only
Trading cryptocurrencies poses considerable risk of loss. The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.
I recommend funding the contract with at least 0.25 ETH to make sure that won't happen.
the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats a proposed minimum deposit and an account of possible profits as though they establish a guaranteed payout. But the funding explanation discusses fees, while the description expressly says outcomes are not guaranteed. The claim that larger trades can produce larger profits describes the speaker's proposed mechanism; it does not establish that every viewer is promised a return.

citations.quote: If you fund the contract with 0.25 ETH or less, and the bot targets another token with high burn fees, the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.
The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning about risk does not change what viewers are asked to do. The speaker directs them to deposit ETH into the bot contract, then connects larger deposits to greater profit. Those operational instructions and the promised opportunity to earn through a funded bot remain central even without an unconditional guarantee.

citations.quote: Deposit funds (at least 0.25 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
the more you put in the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich, and the more profit you'll be able to accumulate over time

opening.argument: The substance of the presentation is a walk-through of a Solidity workflow: the speaker explains how the proposed trading method works, identifies the compiler version, and demonstrates deploying a contract. Those details matter because the viewer is shown a technical process rather than merely told to send money for a payout. The reported returns can be read as the speaker's account of a demonstration, not independent proof that the process will work for every viewer.

citations.quote: Today I'll be teaching you step-by-step how to deploy an Ethereum Trading Bot I've recently developed in the Solidity language
it sniffs the mempool for transactions that are pending within a block
Under Compiler, Select the 0.6.6 version so that it matches our contract.
Sweet, we can see here that it's confirmed, meaning our smart contract is deployed.
So as you can see I have about 1.31 Ethereum which is 31% profit already

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution cites the funding step but gives too little weight to its place in a longer technical walk-through. Explaining a proposed sandwich trade, compiling code, and deploying through a wallet are consistent with demonstrating how a contract is operated. The speaker's claimed result does not by itself prove either that another person's funds will produce that result or that the instruction is a deceptive solicitation.

citations.quote: This will allow us to process our order first, then process a sell order right after, in the same block.
Now that our bot is ready let's compile it.
So as you can see I have about 1.31 Ethereum which is 31% profit already

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical walk-through is the route to the funded offer, not a substitute for it. Viewers are told to put ETH into the contract and start the bot, while the speaker describes daily passive income and displays claimed profits. Showing compilation steps does not establish that the code performs the described trades or that the reported returns arose from them.

citations.quote: Deposit funds (at least 0.25 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
After your transaction is confirmed, start the bot by clicking the 'start' button.
which can make you very easy daily passive income
So as you can see I have about 1.31 Ethereum which is 31% profit already

opening.argument: The instructions describe funding what the presenter calls the viewer's own deployed contract, then using its start and withdrawal controls. The account of the demonstration says the withdrawal returned funds to the wallet. That does not verify the bot's earnings, but it also does not establish that deposits are sent to a separate recipient or made permanently inaccessible. The supplied instructions show no request for wallet credentials or income from recruiting others. On this record, a claimed self-operated trading tool remains a plausible reading.

citations.quote: After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
Deposit funds (at least 0.25 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
Withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into this wallet
As you can see the balance from the bot is now in my wallet!

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution is right that funding is required for the proposed trading workflow. That fact alone does not show who ultimately controls the deposited ETH or whether the withdrawal function works as described. Its cited mempool explanation describes the purported source of trading profit, while the instructions describe a contract the viewer deploys and a withdrawal control. Neither establishes a guaranteed return.

citations.quote: After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
Withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into this wallet
The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it the viewer's bot and naming a withdrawal control does not verify the contract's behavior or establish that deposited funds can be recovered. The instructions still direct viewers to fund the contract and start it, and the speaker explicitly links larger deposits to greater profits. The absence of a credential request or recruitment scheme does not answer that funded-return pitch.
